title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: After reaching home Nicholas was at first serious and even glum. He was weighed down by the looming necessity of dealing with the stupid business matters his mother had called him home for. To get the burden off his back as quickly as possible, on the third day after his arrival he went, angry and scowling and refusing to say where he was going, to Mitenka's lodge and demanded a full accounting. But what a "full accounting" might look like, Nicholas knew even less than the frightened and bewildered Mitenka. The interview and review of the books did not last long. The village elder, a peasant representative, and the village clerk, who were waiting in the corridor, heard with a mixture of fear and delight first the young count's voice roaring and snapping and rising louder and louder, and then foul words — terrible words — erupting one after another.
"Thief!... Ungrateful wretch!... I'll hack the dog to pieces! I'm not my father!... Robbing us!..." and so on.

Then with no less fear and delight they watched the young count, red-faced and with bloodshot eyes, drag Mitenka out by the scruff of his neck and apply his boot and knee to his backside with remarkable agility, timing each kick between the words and shouting: "Get out! Never let me see your face here again, you scoundrel!"

Mitenka flew headlong down the six steps and ran off into the shrubbery. (This shrubbery was a well-known refuge for wrongdoers at Otradnoe. Mitenka himself, returning drunk from town, used to hide there, and many of the residents at Otradnoe, hiding from Mitenka, knew of its protective qualities.)
Mitenka's wife and sisters-in-law poked their heads and frightened faces out the door of a room where a bright samovar was boiling and where the steward's high bed stood with its patchwork quilt.
The young count paid them no attention but, breathing hard, strode past with determination and went into the house.

The countess, who heard at once from the maids what had happened at the lodge, was reassured by the thought that their affairs would surely now improve, but at the same time worried about what the excitement might do to her son. She went several times on tiptoe to his door and listened as he lit one pipe after another.
The next day the old count took his son aside and, with an embarrassed smile, said:
"But you know, my dear boy, it's a shame you lost your temper! Mitenka has told me all about it."
"I knew it," thought Nicholas, "I'd never make sense of anything in this crazy world."
"You were angry because he hadn't entered those seven hundred rubles. But they were carried forward — and you didn't look at the other page."
"Papa, he's a crook and a thief! I know he is! And what I did, I did. But if you prefer, I won't say another word to him."

"No, my dear boy" — the count, too, felt embarrassed; he knew he had mismanaged his wife's property and was to blame toward his children, but he didn't know how to fix it — "No, I beg you to take care of the business. I'm old. I..."
"No, Papa. Forgive me if I've upset you. I understand it all even less than you do."

"To hell with all these peasants, and money matters, and carrying things forward from page to page," he thought. "I used to understand what a 'corner' and the stakes at cards meant, but I don't understand carrying forward at all," he told himself, and after that he didn't meddle in business affairs. But once the countess called her son in and told him that she held a promissory note from Anna Mikhaylovna for two thousand rubles, and asked him what he thought they should do with it.

"This," answered Nicholas. "You say it's up to me. Well, I don't like Anna Mikhaylovna and I don't like Boris, but they were our friends and they're poor. So — this!" And he tore up the note, which made the old countess weep tears of joy. After that, young Rostov took no further part in business affairs and threw himself with passionate enthusiasm into what was for him a new pursuit — hunting — for which his father maintained a large establishment.
